lesson.menu_desc: Asking a curator the right question -- and the follow-up that gets the real answer -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- The Question Behind the Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Liliane Meira | Lesson 9 -- The Question Behind the Question

listenings.text: I record long interviews with nurses, sometimes for three or four hours, and what I have learned is that the first answer is almost never the interesting one. The first answer is the one people have given before, at dinners and in meetings. It is polished, and it is safe. The interesting material starts with the follow-up question, and the best follow-up is usually made of the other person's own words. If a nurse tells me the night shift was hard, I do not ask why. I ask: when you say hard, what did it look like at three in the morning? That takes her back into the room. The other thing I have learned is to stop talking. After a good question, most people need a few seconds of silence before they say the real thing, and the temptation is to rescue them with another question. Do not rescue them. Wait.

There are two questions I have stopped asking artists altogether. The first is: what inspired you? It is so open that it invites a prepared answer, and I get the paragraph from the press release. The second is any question that already contains the answer I want, something like: would you say this work is about loss? That is a leading question, and a polite artist will simply agree with me, which tells me nothing. What I ask instead is concrete. What was on the table in the studio the week you finished it? Which part did you change last? Concrete questions are harder to dodge, and they get me to the ideas faster than abstract ones do. And when somebody does dodge, I do not accuse them. I rephrase the question once, gently. If they dodge it a second time, that is the answer.
